newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Cullen welcomes Brash warning, Peters silent.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Cullen welcomes Brash warning, Peters silent.

text.p: Labour finance spokesman Michael Cullen on Monday welcomed Reserve Bank governor Don Brash's call for the markets not to expect too much certainty, but downplayed Brash's warning against increased spending.
New Zealand First leader Winston Peters said through a spokesman he was aware of the content of Brash's speech but declined to comment.

NZ First, which holds the balance of power after the October 12 election, is negotiating separately with the caretaker conservative National Party and the main opposition Labour Party over the shape of the next government.
Both New Zealand First and Labour are promising increased social spending, but Labour has said it would defer and revamp the tax cuts.
National has said it is committed to the second round of tax cuts. The first round was implemented on July 1 this year.
Brash said on Monday the tax cuts planned for mid-1997 may need to be deferred if government spending rises.

"Coalition partners may indeed need to consider deferring some part of the tax cuts already announced if there is to be any increase in government expenditure," Brash said in a speech to a Federated Farmers meeting in Invercargill.
"Clearly, one direct way of reducing the risk inherent in the present situation would be to ensure that further fiscal stimulus is not added in the process of coalition forming.
"There is obviously a huge problem for political leaders in this situation," Brash said.
"A more realistic understanding on the part of foreign investors of the risks of investing in New Zealand dollar assets would also help," Brash added.

In a statement Cullen said while Brash's speech contained some warnings about increased government spending, it was important financial markets and politicial commentators did not miss the main point.
"In a sense New Zealand is, at the moment, being punished for excessive certainty concerning monetary policy. Over the last 12 years we've seen what's almost a strange reversal in economic policy.
"Where once farmers were guaranteed minimum payments and manufacturers were guaranteed a share of the New Zealand market they now face complete competition and complete uncertainty.

"Those in the financial markets on the other hand demand, crave, expect, and are getting complete certainty. The most dangerous part of that is there is nopw an assumption that the exchange rate will continue to appreciate. This has become a dangerous and dramatically self-fulfilling prophecy as the financial markets act in the expectation that this assumption will be fulfilled," Cullen said.
"The resulting massive over-appreciation in the New Zealand dollar is causing serious harm to farmers, exporters, manufacturers and competitors with imported goods.

"A little uncertainty in the financial markets would go a long way to ensuring that the unjustified and unsustainable rise in the New Zealand dollar which we've seen over the last few weeks is reversed.

"Dr Brash has wisely not waited for the conclusion of the present round of coalition talks to send a clear message to financial markets that they should not bank on absolute certainty with respect to movement of the New Zealand currency.
"The bank is showing a welcome recognition of problems in the real economy and it is to be hoped that the financial markets act accordingly," Cullen said.
